objection: If Jesus is God, why did he pray to God?
answer:
Gethsemane is real, and I won't soften it: Jesus genuinely asks the Father, as a man, to let the cup pass. But notice what this actually requires. The passages here show the same Jesus who prays in John 17:3, distinguishing Himself from the Father, is confessed by that same Gospel as the Word who was God and worshipped by Thomas as "my Lord and my God." One Gospel holds both without embarrassment. That's not incoherence; it's the shape of incarnation. The Son who eternally possesses the divine nature has, in becoming man, taken a genuine human nature complete with a human will, a human mind, and human affections — including the capacity to be sorrowful, to shrink from suffering, to petition. Philippians 2 describes exactly this: one who existed in the form of God emptied Himself, took the form of a servant, and was truly human. Gethsemane is the "true humanity" clause of that hymn playing out in real time.

As for the "righteous sufferer later deified" theory — the material here suggests the deification, if that's what it was, happened remarkably early and remarkably boldly. The earliest Christians didn't just revere Jesus' memory; they addressed him directly in prayer, as Stephen does in Acts 7:59, and used the Aramaic invocation Maranatha (1 Corinthians 16:22), a formula so early it predates Greek-speaking Christianity. Paul, writing decades before any council, applies the Isaiah 45 language of universal, exclusive worship of YHWH to Jesus without any sense of conflict (Philippians 2:9-11). That's not slow legendary accretion; it's worship built into the foundation.

So the two-wills language isn't a later patch over an embarrassing text — it's the only way to hold together, without contradiction, a Jesus who prays to the Father in Gethsemane and a Jesus to whom the apostolic church prayed at the Lord's table. The objection rightly insists we take the prayer seriously; Nicene Christology insists we take it exactly as seriously as we take Thomas's confession.

# Historical-Critical Objection: The Prayer Problem

Look, if Jesus *is* God in the full sense — coequal, consubstantial, sharing one divine nature — then what are we to make of Gethsemane? "Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me" — that's petition, subordination, a will distinct from and asking the will of another. Paul can say he is "in Christ," but Christ praying *to* someone else reads like a creature addressing his superior, not the second person of the Godhead addressing the first. The Nicene framers knew this problem, which is why they had to invent *two wills* — one divine, one human — but that's metaphysical gymnastics nowhere in Mark or Q. Couldn't the simpler reading be that Jesus was a supremely devoted human, a *righteous sufferer* in the Psalms tradition, who prayed because he was human? That his followers later deified him, as they deified their memory of his faith?

Let me take the objection seriously, because Gethsemane is precisely the place where a cheap, docetic Christology collapses — and precisely the place the material here actually addresses.

Notice first that John 17:3, the very prayer where Jesus distinguishes Himself from "the only true God," occurs in the same Gospel that opens by calling the Word God and closes with Thomas confessing the risen Jesus as "my Lord and my God." John does not experience any tension in recording both the Son's prayer to the Father and the Son's deity — because the distinction pressed in prayer is a distinction of *persons*, not a demotion of *nature*. The Son address the Father as other than Himself in every prayer, including Gethsemane, precisely because the Father and Son are eternally distinct persons within the one God. That personal distinction is what makes it a Trinity and not a solitary monad; it was never in tension with consubstantiality, only with modalism.

What Gethsemane adds is the human will, the genuinely human anguish, the "if it be possible" of a real man facing real death. That's not gymnastics invented to patch a problem — it's what you'd expect if the eternal Son "existed in the form of God" and then genuinely "humbled Himself," taking true humanity, as Philippians 2 puts it. A nature capable of suffering, fearing, and petitioning is exactly what the incarnation requires; without it the cross is theater. The two-wills language just names, formally, what the prayer itself already shows: a divine person willing, as God, the salvation of the world, while his human nature, as man, shrinks from the cup and submits to the Father's will.

As for "a righteous sufferer later deified by devotion" — that reading has to explain why the earliest Christians, within a generation, were praying to Jesus as Lord (Acts 7:59, 1 Corinthians 16:22), applying to Him the worship Isaiah 45 reserves for YHWH alone (Philippians 2:9–11), and hearing the Father Himself addressed as speaking to the Son as God (Hebrews's citation of Psalm 45:6, per Colossians 1's larger portrait of the Son as Creator and Sustainer). That is not the trajectory of memory inflating a devout teacher; it is worship offered immediately and without apology to the crucified man they had watched pray in Gethsemane. The prayer and the worship sit in the same texts, from the same writers, without felt contradiction — because for them the one praying "Father, let this cup pass" was never less than the one to whom every knee bows.
